title: Model Collapse: Recursive Training on Your Own Output

questions.question: A model is refit each generation on n samples drawn only from the previous generation's model. Which quantity is preserved in expectation, and which is not?
options: Entropy is preserved in expectation; each category's probability is not
Each category's probability is preserved in expectation; entropy is not
Both entropy and each category's probability are preserved in expectation
Neither entropy nor any category's probability is preserved in expectation
questions.explanation: Resampling makes every category frequency a martingale (E[p_hat(g+1) | p_hat(g)] = p_hat(g)), while entropy is strictly concave, so by Jensen it is a supermartingale that falls in expectation every generation.

questions.question: A category has probability p = 0.001 and the loop resamples n = 1000 items per generation with no smoothing. Roughly what is the chance it vanishes in one resample, and what happens afterwards?
options: About 0.1%, and it returns as soon as the model is refit on the next sample
About 37%, and it returns in the next generation with the same probability
About 37%, and it never returns because its fitted probability is now zero
About 63%, and it returns only if the loop switches to accumulating data
questions.explanation: P[zero draws] = (1 - p)^n ≈ e^(-np) = e^(-1) ≈ 0.37. With no smoothing the empirical model assigns it probability 0, so it can never be sampled again: extinction is absorbing.

questions.question: Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) report that accumulating data avoids collapse. In the simulator, why does the extinct count stay frozen at its generation-0 value under the accumulate regime?
options: The real generation-0 sample never leaves the training pool, so none of its categories can reach zero count
The synthetic generations are reweighted each time so that every category receives at least one count
Accumulation lowers the sampling noise enough that no category ever draws zero samples in n draws
The regime refits on the truth distribution directly instead of on samples, so nothing is ever lost
questions.explanation: Accumulate fits on real gen-0 data plus every synthetic generation; the real counts are never discarded, so a category present at gen 0 always has at least its original count. Categories missing at gen 0 stay missing.

questions.question: Under the replace regime the tail mass (rank > 100) stayed near 0.085–0.090 for 20 generations while the number of living tail categories fell from 85 to 12. What does this imply for monitoring?
options: Tail mass is the right monitor because it is stable and therefore reliable across generations
The two numbers contradict each other, so the simulation has a bug in the tail-mass computation
Collapse has not started yet, because the share of rare content in the model is unchanged
Mass is conserved in expectation but concentrates on survivors, so track alive or distinct counts, not mass
questions.explanation: The sum of martingales is a martingale, so tail mass is preserved in expectation while the categories carrying it go extinct one by one. Extinct count, tail-alive count and distinct@k see the collapse; mass does not.

questions.question: Yue et al. (NeurIPS 2025) found RL-trained models beat their base models at pass@1 but lose at pass@k for large k. In this lesson's terms, what happened?
options: The RL model learned new reasoning paths the base lacked, so its support grew while its head shrank
The RL model moved probability onto paths the base already preferred, so its head rose while its support shrank
The base model's pass@k is inflated by memorisation, so the comparison says nothing about diversity
The RL model's verifier filtered out wrong answers, so its support is strictly larger than the base model's
questions.explanation: pass@k = 1 - (1 - p)^k rewards support, not peak probability. Sharpening onto already-preferred paths raises pass@1 and lowers pass@k at large k, the same signature as finite-sample collapse of the tail.

questions.question: A team proposes a mix policy: 'cap synthetic data at 80%, since Seddik et al. show a maximal synthetic fraction exists.' What is the strongest objection from this lesson?
options: Seddik et al. showed that no amount of real data can prevent collapse, so the cap is meaningless
An 80% cap is far too loose; the lesson shows that any synthetic share above 20% collapses immediately
The maximal fraction depends on n and on the tail of the data; it must be measured at the loop's own n, not quoted
Caps are unnecessary when data accumulates, so the team should drop the cap and keep every generation
questions.explanation: In the simulator rho = 0.2 (80% synthetic) held TV near 0.13 at n = 2000 but lost 14.5% of entropy and 123 categories at n = 500. The cap must come from a sweep at the loop's actual sample size and tail, with provenance tags to enforce it.
